title: Toldot: room at last (Genesis 26:18–22)
hookLine: wells named Quarrel and Enmity, then Rehoboth, broad places

cards: The parking spot. The armrest on the plane. The neighbor's hedge, six inches over the line.
Some fights are about real things. A lot of them are about who gets the space. Isaac, grown now, lives among the Philistines in a dry land, where water is everything.
His father Abraham once dug wells there, and since then they've been stopped up with earth. So Isaac starts digging. And every time he finds water, somebody shows up to claim it.

teach.h: HIS FATHER'S WELLS, HIS FATHER'S NAMES.
teach.b: First, Isaac digs again the wells of his father, and here's a tender detail: he calls them by the same names his father had called them. Then his servants dig in the valley and find living water, a spring.
The herdsmen of Gerar come and say: the water is ours. Isaac names that well Esek, contention. Quarrel.
And he moves on. Another well, another fight.
He names that one Sitnah, enmity, and moves on again. Notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't fight for either well.
He gives each one an honest name, a record of what happened there, and he walks. Then they dig a third well, and this time, the text says, they didn't strive for it.

He names it Rehoboth, from the Hebrew for broad, wide, open spaces. And he says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "For now the LORD hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land."
Room, the gift at the end of all that digging. The medieval commentator Ramban read the three wells as a picture of Jewish history: two fought over, and a third, in the future, with room at last.
Other readers keep it close to home. Some fights aren't worth winning. Moving on isn't the same as losing.
And there's usually a Rehoboth somewhere, if you're willing to keep digging.

teach.h: THE KING COMES ASKING FOR PEACE.
teach.b: Then the surprise: the king of the Philistines comes to Isaac and asks for a treaty.

teach.h: THE LORD HATH MADE ROOM FOR US.
teach.b: The man who walked away twice ends up with peace.

how: Jewish teaching prizes pursuing peace and avoiding needless quarrels, machloket, and Rehovot, a city in Israel, takes its name from Isaac's well of broad places.

generations, the story of a family line
wells, the water Isaac dug up again

games.q: what's inside the wells — tap the pairs.

s: Isaac fought the herdsmen for the first two wells
he named each one and moved on.
the third well was named for having room
Rehoboth: the LORD hath made room for us.
the story ends with the Philistine king asking for a treaty
the king came to Isaac and asked to make a covenant of peace.

games.q: you've dug a well in a dry land and found water. the local herdsmen say it's theirs. you're Isaac. what do you do?
o: fight for it: you dug it.
name it quarrel, and dig somewhere else.
share it and hope for the best.
games.why: Isaac named it Esek, quarrel, and moved on, twice, until he found Rehoboth, where nobody fought, and there was room.

practice: Think of one running quarrel in your life: a group chat argument, a turf war at work, a family thing about who's right. Ask yourself honestly whether it's a well worth fighting for, or an Esek.
If it's an Esek, picture yourself naming it and walking on, breathing into the open space on the other side.

wordCard.voice: Toldot. Generations: the portion where Isaac digs his father's wells, walks away from two fights, and finds Rehoboth, room at last.

orig.note: Hebrew: broad places, wide spaces. the well where there was room at last.

carryVoice: Your line: there's room. Isaac found it at the third well he dug. See you tomorrow.
